prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which atoms trapped at the magic wavelength opened a new regime of precision in the measurement of time

statement.case_for: I keep B001 alone, and the round-1 exchange has sharpened rather than weakened my reason. The chair asked for a sentence on what the lattice clock showed that the comb (2005) and the ion-clock work (2012) did not. My answer is this: the magic-wavelength condition makes the trap light shift cancel between the two clock levels, so a large ensemble of neutral atoms can be interrogated simultaneously while the systematic uncertainty reaches the level previously available only with a single trapped ion. That is both a new physical condition and a new regime, with the statistical advantage of many atoms (stability) and the ion-level control of shifts (accuracy) in one object. The comb gave a way to count optical cycles and the ion work gave control of one quantum system; neither gave this. The evidence is the kind I trust: independent laboratories in Japan, the US, Europe and China build their own lattice clocks and their mutual comparisons agree at the 1e-18 level, and the same instruments have resolved gravitational redshift over millimetre height differences. Those are measurements that were not possible before, which is the criterion I weigh most. The two-name credit is the cleanest on the shortlist, and the citation should name the magic-wavelength lattice explicitly so that the prize cannot be read as a second award for combs.
statement.case_against: Distinctness remains the real risk and I cannot make it vanish by argument, because Danielsson, Eriksson and Mehlig are entitled to read the lattice clock as a superb instrument whose conceptual novelty beyond the magic-wavelength idea is limited. Ye's name also sits in the comb lineage. Second, a two-name prize leaves out Lemonde, Ludlow, Lemke, Takamoto, Derevianko and Bloom, and the record accuracy is shared among laboratories and will be superseded, so the citation must not rest on a number. Third, the redefinition of the second is still pending. After the exchange I am more convinced that this is not a reason to wait, since the redefinition depends on the achievement and not the reverse, but I accept that others may weigh it differently. Finally, B024 has the broadest ranking support, and I have to say honestly that my first place is partly a judgement about measurement, which not everyone shares.

responses.point: Danielsson moved topological insulators to the top as a theory-meets-experiment arc (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) confirmed over fifteen years, noted that seven of eight members rank it, and earlier asked whether lattice clocks are a distinct discovery or a continuation of the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: I take his distinctness question as the central one and I have tried to answer it in one sentence in my case: the new element is the magic-wavelength cancellation, which lets many neutral atoms reach ion-level systematics, and that is not contained in the comb or in single-ion control. I also accept his point on B024 that theory confronted with nature and surviving independent tests over fifteen years is exactly the pattern the prize rewards, and I would not obstruct it on scientific grounds. Where I still differ is the allocation: he himself says the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang omission and Hasan's 3D work are real costs, and I find that a prize with an uncontested two-name credit is easier to defend than one where any trio omits a decisive contributor. Breadth of support in the opening ballots is a useful signal, but I do not treat it as scientific weight.

responses.point: Mehlig argues that an organising concept (the bulk Z2 invariant and bulk-boundary correspondence) that changed how materials are searched outweighs an instrument whose conceptual novelty beyond the magic-wavelength idea is smaller, and that HgTe edge conductance and ARPES are quantitative confirmations.
responses.response: He is right that HgTe conductance of 2e^2/h and the ARPES Dirac cones are precise measurements, and I withdraw my earlier phrasing that the topic is less measurement-oriented. I disagree on the weighting: the magic-wavelength idea is itself a general condition (any species with a suitable level structure can be engineered to a magic wavelength), and its reach is shown by the range of atoms and the many-body and relativistic studies now done with lattice clocks, even though it touches fewer communities than topology. My concern with B024 is the same one he names, namely that Kane, Mele and Molenkamp omit Hasan and the HgTe theory proposers, and I think a three-name limit makes that cost unavoidable. If the committee converges on B024 I would support Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as the least bad trio, but I would not move B024 above B001 on the evidence in these statements.

responses.point: Eriksson accepts the clean credit and the independent confirmation for lattice clocks but, as a condensed-matter physicist, asks whether atomic physicists see a distinct physical discovery, such as many-body effects, rather than excellent engineering.
responses.response: I answer as the atomic physicist he asks for. The magic wavelength is a physical discovery in the sense that it identifies a condition under which a perturbation as strong as a trapping potential leaves the transition frequency unperturbed to first order, which was not obvious and was not an engineering refinement. Beyond that, the lattice clock is now an instrument for many-body physics: Ye's group has observed interaction and collective effects that are controlled and then used, so the ensemble is not a passive counting device. I do not claim it is a new state of matter, and if the committee requires that, B001 will not satisfy it. I also share his hesitation about B013, since the pairing mechanism and twist-angle disorder are not yet settled, so maturity is a point where B001 is clearly stronger.

responses.point: Pearce pairs B001 with IceCube (Halzen alone) as two distinct instrument-driven achievements, and asks me whether the pending redefinition of the second troubles me if B001 is paired with something else.
responses.response: On his question: the redefinition does not trouble me, because the demonstrated performance and the cross-laboratory agreement are already in hand, and the redefinition is a metrological decision that depends on them. I would not wait for it, and I would not make the citation rest on it. On the pairing I remain unconvinced by the IceCube half for the reason he gives himself as the weakest link: one name for a collaboration of hundreds with AMANDA and DUMAND predecessors, and the source classes behind the diffuse flux are not settled. A single-name credit makes the pairing look like a compromise to give the prize three names. I would rather he considered B001 alone than attach a part whose credit he cannot defend publicly. If the committee wants two parts, I would need a different second part, not one whose attribution is the open question.

responses.point: Johansson prefers Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan for B024 so that the 3D topological insulator observation is recognised, and says the case weakens if the committee will not accept Hasan or the omission of Mele.
responses.response: I find his concern about leaving the 3D observation unrecognised real, and it shows why I do not think B024 can be made uncontroversial: Mehlig and Danielsson hold that Mele cannot be separated from Kane, while he holds that Hasan cannot be left out, and both positions are defensible on the record. That disagreement among the condensed-matter members is not a problem I can resolve from the atomic side, and it is a reason I would not subordinate the clean B001 credit to it. I do thank him for stating plainly that the case weakens without a defensible trio, since it is the same standard I apply to B001, where the credit does not depend on a choice between equally strong claimants.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the magic-wavelength lattice with many-atom ion-level systematics as distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-clock prizes; this is a judgement and the colleagues who doubt it have a fair point.
I still rely on memory for the most recent uncertainty figures and the status of the second-redefinition roadmap, which is why I want the citation to avoid a specific number or date.
Whether a two-name prize is fair to Lemonde, Ludlow, Lemke, Takamoto and Derevianko, and whether the committee prefers to put the weight on the proposal or on the accuracy frontier.
If the committee prefers B024, I cannot judge whether Kane, Mele and Molenkamp or Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan is the fairer trio, and I would defer to the condensed-matter members on that.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1, and as I stated, not obviously disqualifying: during my PhD I spent a year in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Jun Ye is at JILA, where Hall worked, but I have no joint work, supervision or funding relationship with Ye or Katori. My background in precision laser spectroscopy and quantum optics places me close to the field of B001, so the committee should weigh my first-place preference with that in mind and may reasonably count it with that reservation. I am also on the management team of a spin-off company and the WACQT quantum-sensing programme, neither of which has any link to the credited names.
